summary:
Radar snapshot for 2026-10-11, 20:18 UTC. Channel focus: plague.

The news cycle has moved on. It is no longer "suspected plague case." It is now "an unresolved death, and WHO is still asking questions."

Dated developments, each credited to the body that spoke. Re-check them all at publish time.
- **Oct 6:** Russia told WHO no plague case had been recorded.
- **Oct 8:** Rospotrebnadzor rejected reports of a second case (AP).
- **Oct 8 or 9:** Irkutsk oblast governor Igor Kobzev said about 5,000 lab tests found no dangerous pathogens and that restrictions were lifted. Bloomberg, Kyiv Post and Kyiv Independent all reported this. Sources disagree on Oct 8 vs Oct 9, so confirm the date from the original. Keep AP's caveat that he did not say whether pneumonic plague was ruled out.
- **Oct 10:** WHO officials said it is still unclear what caused the pneumonia and how she was infected, and asked for more information (Reuters, ABC). Reuters' headline also says "plague-lab worker," so double-check the wording.
- **Oct 11:** New coverage keeps coming from AP, NYT, the Washington Post, SBS and FT. The CDC director appeared on Fox. Earlier, CDC called the US risk "extremely low" (Axios, Oct 6).

Mainstream explainers ("what is pneumonic plague") are now everywhere: NBC, CNN, PBS, WUNC, Pharmacy Times, Contagion Live and others. That makes generic Plague 101 high-competition. Our edge is narrower, search-shaped angles that start with "Plague", name an agency and pay off fast.

**Best near-term openings**
1. A dated Short and long-form that decode the status: "WHO says cause still unknown" versus "Russia says no plague."
2. Why a lab can take days to identify the pathogen behind a pneumonia death, using CDC's presumptive-vs-confirmed definition. This is emerging and few creators cover it.
3. How contact monitoring ends, built on WHO's seven-day chemoprophylaxis and the incubation period.
4. The documented 2009 Chicago lab-acquired plague case (CDC MMWR, 2011), a low-competition lab-safety story backed by a primary source.
5. Plague vaccine status. There's a news hook, but the science needs careful scoping.
6. The WHO reporting rules (International Health Regulations) explained neutrally, since NPR has raised the question.

Seasonal hook: Madagascar's plague season runs roughly August–April, so place-based Shorts in our proven "Plague in [place] + agency number" format stay relevant.

Evergreen search questions still drive volume, though the "person to person" topic is slowly losing momentum after 8 snapshots. These are: person to person, symptoms, curable, US cases, pneumonic vs bubonic plague, and plague vs COVID.

Reject: bioweapon, lab-leak and cover-up framing (Euronews, Washington Post and Newsmax opinion pieces are pushing it), stories about the family's claims about the person who died, "permafrost scarier than plague" fear content, and antibiotic stockpiling.

Caution: the European Medical Journal "vaccine shows promise" headline. I couldn't verify the underlying study, and the evidence I found is from animal studies.

candidates.topic: Plague status decoder, as of Oct 10–11, 2026: WHO says the cause of the Irkutsk oblast lab worker's pneumonia is still unclear; Russia says no plague case was registered; the governor reported about 5,000 negative tests and lifted restrictions
candidates.angle: 'Plague in Russia: what's confirmed, what's reported, what's still unknown (as of Oct 11, 2026).' Open with the newest item: WHO, Oct 10, cause and route of infection still unclear, more information requested. Then add dated lines in order, each credited to its body: Oct 6, Russia told WHO no plague case was recorded. Oct 8, Rospotrebnadzor rejected reports of a second case (AP). Oct 8–9, the governor reported about 5,000 lab tests with no dangerous pathogens and lifted restrictions, plus AP's caveat that he did not say whether pneumonic plague was ruled out. CDC: US risk 'extremely low'. Don't end on the most reassuring line; end on what WHO is still waiting for. Use 'not confirmed', never 'ruled out'. Close with the urgent-contact line.
candidates.predicted_peak: now to 3 days; long search tail for 1–2 weeks with each new WHO statement
candidates.why_now: The newest development, WHO officials on Oct 10 saying it's still unclear what caused the death (Reuters, ABC), has been reported for under 36 hours, and new coverage kept coming on Oct 11 (AP, NYT, Washington Post, SBS, Independent). The playbook names this exact decoder as the next plague long-form and the breaking-news Short format. Re-check WHO, Rospotrebnadzor and CDC at publish time.

evidence.signal: WHO unsure what caused pneumonia that killed plague-lab worker in Russia
WHO wants more answers from Russia; says it doesn't know the cause or how she was infected
Russia's public health watchdog denies a second infection
Russia lifts quarantine in Irkutsk region after governor reports tests with no dangerous pathogens
CDC: risk to US 'extremely low'; prepared and monitoring

candidates.topic: Plague testing explained: why the cause of a severe pneumonia can stay 'undetermined' for days, and what 'presumptive' vs 'confirmed' plague means (CDC case definition)
candidates.angle: 'Plague tests: why it can take days to know (CDC).' Use the news only as one neutral line of context, e.g. WHO said on Oct 10 the cause is still unclear. Then explain settled science. CDC's 2020 case definition: PCR, antigen or F1 rapid tests make a case 'presumptive'. 'Confirmed' means Y. pestis grown in culture or a fourfold rise in antibodies. Explain why culture takes time and why doctors start antibiotics before results come back. Don't cite CDC's 'Clinical Testing and Diagnosis' page for PCR or culture time.
keywords: why don't they know what killed her
candidates.why_now: The main public question has shifted from 'is it plague?' to 'why don't they know yet?' (NYT, Oct 10: 'A week later, Russia hasn't said what pathogen killed…'; WHO, Oct 10: cause unclear). Almost no creators explain diagnostic confirmation, and it answers the search question without speculating about the case.

evidence.source: New York Times via Google News (Oct 10)
evidence.signal: A Week Later, Russia Hasn't Said What Pathogen Killed Plague Researcher
Russia says 'pneumonia of unknown origin'
'Pneumonic plague or pneumonia?' framing is spreading

candidates.topic: Lab-acquired plague in the US: the 2009 Chicago case (CDC MMWR, 2011). A researcher working with a weakened (attenuated) Y. pestis strain died; he had undiagnosed hereditary hemochromatosis (iron overload)
candidates.angle: 'Plague in a US lab: what CDC learned from a 2009 case.' A documented, peer-reviewed case study in calm detail. A weakened strain was considered low-risk. Iron overload likely let it cause severe infection. CDC concluded the likely cause was an unrecognized occupational exposure. Then explain what labs changed and why lab exposures get medical follow-up. Use only MMWR wording. No link to the Irkutsk case beyond one neutral context line. Don't lead with the person's name.
candidates.why_now: Céline Gounder published a 2009 Chicago vs 2026 Irkutsk comparison on Oct 10. Interest in 'can lab workers catch plague' is high, and the primary source (CDC MMWR) is solid and public. Very few videos cover it. It fits the lab-safety pillar.

evidence.signal: Fatal Laboratory-Acquired Infection with an Attenuated Yersinia pestis Strain, Chicago, Illinois, 2009
Full MMWR record
Lab-acquired plague: the 2009 Chicago case and the 2026 Irkutsk death

candidates.topic: Plague contact monitoring: why observation lasts about a week, and how preventive antibiotics (WHO: 'seven-day chemoprophylaxis') and isolation stop pneumonic plague spreading
candidates.angle: 'Plague exposure: what health authorities do next (WHO, CDC).' Hook: reports say observation of about 200 contacts in Irkutsk oblast has ended. Credit this to the body that said it, dated. Explain the settled logic: the pneumonic incubation period (CDC wording), why monitoring windows match it, preventive antibiotics given by health authorities, isolation, and Madagascar 2017 as the real example. Never suggest self-treatment. Close with the urgent-contact line.
candidates.why_now: The quarantine was lifted and contact observation ended Oct 8–9 (governor and Rospotrebnadzor, via Kyiv Post, Bloomberg and Kyiv Independent). That raises a direct search question: why did monitoring end, and how long does it need to last? It refreshes the Madagascar topic (8 snapshots, slowly declining) with a news hook. It's the playbook's 'you-action' title format.

evidence.signal: Russia Ends Irkutsk Health Measures as Tests Find No Pathogens
Russia Ends Irkutsk Quarantine Despite Unresolved Plague Questions
Testing and monitoring underway in suspected Russia plague death

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague: can it spread person to person? CDC says through respiratory droplets during direct, close contact, unlike truly airborne measles
candidates.angle: 'Pneumonic plague: can it spread person to person? (CDC, WHO).' Answer within 10 seconds using CDC's 'requires direct and close contact' and 'can sometimes cough droplets'. Add the contrast with measles. Bubonic plague is not normally passed between people.
keywords: can plague spread person to person
candidates.why_now: This is still the top search question, and it has appeared in 8 of our snapshots. Momentum is slowly falling (90 down to 86), but every new headline keeps refreshing it. Mainstream explainers cover it, but rarely with exact agency wording in a 60-second answer.

evidence.signal: What is pneumonic plague, and how is it transmitted?
Pneumonic plague, by the numbers
What is the pneumonic plague?

candidates.topic: Plague vaccine in 2026: is there one? No licensed plague vaccine for the public in the US; Russia uses a live vaccine for at-risk workers; next-generation vaccines are in animal and early-stage research
candidates.angle: 'Plague vaccine: is there one? (WHO, CDC).' News hook: the governor reportedly said she had been vaccinated. Credit this to him, dated. Then settled facts: what is and isn't licensed, where each vaccine is used, why WHO and CDC rely on antibiotics and preventive antibiotics for contacts. Don't mix up findings about killed and live vaccines (a past scope hold). Animal results must be labeled as animal studies.
keywords: is there a vaccine for plague
candidates.why_now: The European Medical Journal ran 'Pneumonic Plague Vaccine Shows Promise' on Oct 10, and the governor's vaccination claim is circulating. Few creators cover vaccine status accurately. I couldn't verify the underlying study, and the evidence I found is from animal studies, so wording must stay tightly hedged.

evidence.source: European Medical Journal via Google News (Oct 10)
evidence.signal: Pneumonic Plague Vaccine Shows Promise Amidst Russian Outbreak
Nasal vaccine shows promise as booster against pneumonic plague (animal research, Nature Communications)
Governor said the worker had been vaccinated (attribute only)

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague symptoms and timing: fever, cough, shortness of breath and chest pain (CDC), typically appearing within days of exposure, and when to get urgent care
candidates.angle: 'Plague symptoms: when to get urgent care (CDC).' List all 4 pneumonic signs in CDC's wording, the incubation period in CDC's wording, and who is actually at risk (possible exposure, travel to or living in areas where plague occurs). Then 'contact a doctor or local health authority urgently'. Calm: a cough alone is not plague.
candidates.why_now: Steady top-3 search intent across 7 snapshots (80 to 86 to 84). Every news peak sends people searching for symptoms, and Pharmacy Times and Contagion Live FAQs show professional demand too.

evidence.signal: Pneumonic plague: symptoms, antibiotics and current US risk
FAQ: Pneumonic Plague
What to know about plague

candidates.topic: Plague and global health rules: what the International Health Regulations require countries to report to WHO, and how WHO verifies a suspected event
candidates.angle: 'Plague and WHO rules: what countries must report.' A neutral civics explainer of the IHR (2005): the notification duty, WHO's verification requests, and why WHO asks for pathogen details. One neutral line saying WHO has publicly requested more information. No blame, no stigma, no cover-up framing.
keywords: does Russia have to report plague to WHO
candidates.why_now: NPR asked 'Did Russia play by the rules in reporting?' on Oct 9. Japan, the EU, Thailand and Central Asian countries have sought information. It's an explanatory gap: lots of opinion pieces, few plain explainers. Because of the stigma and politics risk it needs strict neutrality.

evidence.signal: Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
Japan seeks info from Russia after Irkutsk lab worker dies
WHO urges formal response

candidates.topic: Plague in the US: CDC says an average of five human cases are reported each year (range 0–17), mostly in the rural West, with pet, flea and wildlife prevention
candidates.angle: 'Plague in the US: how many human cases a year (CDC).' Our best-performing format. Copy CDC's live wording at publish time. Include pets and fleas with 'follow the label; some dog flea products (e.g. permethrin) are toxic to cats', and 'not documented in the US since 1924' for person-to-person spread, in CDC's exact wording.
keywords: how many plague cases in the US
candidates.predicted_peak: steady; refreshed by each news wave
candidates.why_now: PBS ('The plague never went away… U.S. nearly every year', Oct 9) and Axios ('Here's where plague strikes most', Oct 9) refreshed this angle. Our version got 69 YouTube views, 107 Instagram reach and our first shares. A rerun or variant should re-check the CDC page.

evidence.signal: The plague never went away. Cases reported in parts of Africa and the U.S. nearly every year
Here's where plague strikes most

candidates.topic: Plague in Madagascar: the seasonal plague period (roughly August to April) and how the 2017 pneumonic outbreak was stopped with contact tracing and preventive antibiotics
candidates.angle: 'Plague in Madagascar: why cases rise this time of year (WHO).' This is the 'place + agency number + prevention' format applied to the country WHO most often cites. The season is under way now. Credit every number to WHO's 2017 reports. Don't stigmatize.
candidates.why_now: Axios and PBS 'where plague strikes most' pieces, plus SCMP's 'The plague isn't history' (Oct 10), are driving where-is-it-now searches. Madagascar's plague season is under way. This gives the existing Madagascar topic (8 snapshots, slowly declining) a fresh, timely title.

evidence.signal: The plague isn't history. Where it still exists, how it spreads and a cure
Where plague strikes most

candidates.topic: Is plague curable? CDC: 'Plague can be cured with antibiotics, but treatment must be given quickly'
candidates.angle: 'Plague: is it curable? What CDC and WHO actually say.' Use CDC's exact sentence. Explain why timing matters most for pneumonic plague, and correct the 'no cure' myth. No drug names with doses, no stockpiling. Close with the urgent-contact line.
candidates.why_now: FT's 'Don't panic about the plague' and Irish Medical Times (Oct 10) are pushing reassurance-seeking searches. Our earlier version reached 102 accounts on Instagram, a proven signal.

evidence.signal: Don't panic about the plague
CDC: plague treatable with common antibiotics, especially when treatment starts early

candidates.topic: Pneumonic plague vs bubonic plague: same bacterium (Yersinia pestis), different route, and why only pneumonic passes between people
candidates.angle: 'Pneumonic plague vs bubonic plague: what's the difference? (CDC).' Rebuild the failed carousel as a Short. Name both sides. Add septicemic as the third form. Use WHO's 'case-fatality ratio for the bubonic type' wording if you cite numbers.
candidates.why_now: News uses 'pneumonic' throughout, so people search for the difference. The playbook says to rebuild this as a Short. Five snapshots, holding steady at 74–78.

evidence.source: Health and Me via Google News (Oct 9)
evidence.signal: The Black Death bacterium still exists: forms explained
FAQ on plague forms

candidates.topic: Plague vs COVID: how each spreads, and why experts say global pneumonic plague spread is unlikely
candidates.angle: 'Plague vs COVID: how each one spreads (CDC).' Name both sides: close-contact droplets plus available antibiotics, versus an airborne virus. Quote experts only as attributed, e.g. 'Global pneumonic plague outbreak unlikely, experts say'. No 'pandemic' in the title.
candidates.why_now: Irish Medical Times ('Plague is not the pandemic threat…') and Daily Observer ('Global pneumonic plague outbreak unlikely') show the comparison question is live. The former White House COVID coordinator's comments on NewsNation keep pairing the two.

evidence.source: Irish Medical Times via Google News (Oct 10)
evidence.signal: Plague is not the pandemic threat we should be worrying about
Global pneumonic plague outbreak unlikely, experts say

candidates.topic: How high-containment labs that study plague keep it contained: biosafety levels (BMBL), protective equipment, and what happens after a possible lab exposure
candidates.angle: 'Plague labs: how scientists stay safe (BMBL).' Settled practice from BMBL (updated Mar 18, 2026). Cover which work needs BSL-2 vs BSL-3, PPE, exposure reporting, medical follow-up and preventive antibiotics given by occupational health. Make no claims about Irkutsk beyond one neutral context line. Pairs well with the 2009 Chicago case.
candidates.why_now: Washington Post ('What happened inside Russia's plague lab?', Oct 11) and UnHerd (Oct 10) are pushing lab-safety curiosity, mostly through speculative framing. A calm, factual explainer has little competition. It has appeared in 4 snapshots, steady at 70–74.

evidence.source: Washington Post Opinion via Google News (Oct 11)
evidence.signal: What happened inside Russia's plague lab?
Documented lab-acquired case informs biosafety practice

candidates.topic: Black Death vs plague today: what antibiotics, germ theory and public health changed
candidates.angle: 'Plague then and now: Black Death vs 2026 (WHO).' A history pillar with a hopeful payoff. Use one neutral context line about the news. No doom framing or skull imagery.
keywords: could the Black Death happen again
candidates.why_now: Several outlets (India Today, Health and Me, SCMP) frame the story as 'the Black Death bacterium still exists'. Five snapshots, slowly declining (70 to 66). Good for long-form or a Short when a slot needs filling.

evidence.signal: The plague never left, we just stopped looking

candidates.topic: Plague bioweapon, lab-leak and cover-up theories about the Irkutsk case (including 'worse than plague' and permafrost-pathogen speculation)
candidates.angle: Do not produce. This breaks the niche guardrails: no bioweapon, deliberate-release or cover-up speculation, and no fear-bait. Myth Shorts should correct only the medical beliefs ('no cure', 'airborne like COVID').
candidates.why_now: Euronews, Washington Post and UnHerd opinion pieces and Newsmax are amplifying it. Flagged so downstream agents avoid it.

candidates.angle: Do not produce. The niche guardrails require respect for the person who died and no blame, and these are unverified accounts. At most, a status decoder may say that reports of a lab accident were denied by Russian authorities, attributed and dated.
